intro: You have arrived at Hattusa, an ancient city in Çorum province dating from the 17th century BC. This was the capital of the Hittite Empire, famed for its lion gates and its rock sanctuary.
history: Anatolia's first great empire was ruled from here. Its archives held the Treaty of Kadesh — the earliest known written peace treaty. Think about that for a moment: one of the first written attempts at peace was kept right here.
structure-1: Now you stand before the Lion Gate, the south-west gate in the Upper City wall of the Hittite capital. Between two towers, huge jamb stones lean towards each other until they meet in a parabolic arch, and two lions are cut from the stone of the outer jambs. The wall runs along the crest of an earthen rampart, and the road climbs to the gate along its face on a ramp.
structure-2: You are now at the King's Gate, the city's monumental royal gate. It symbolised the sovereign's entry. Picture the king passing beneath it.
structure-3: And here is the Yerkapı tunnel, the 70-metre monumental tunnel passing beneath the walls of Hattusa. Step into its shadow and feel the weight of the walls above you.
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the Great Temple, and be sure to visit Yazılıkaya.
facts: Did you know? A copy of the Treaty of Kadesh hangs on a wall at the United Nations. Hattusa was the capital of the Hittite Empire, ringed by six kilometres of wall, and the 70-metre stone tunnel under Yerkapı can still be walked through today. The Hittite copy of the Treaty of Kadesh was found here — the oldest known written peace treaty, with a replica on display at the UN in New York. And on the rock walls of the Yazılıkaya open-air sanctuary, more than sixty gods walk in procession.
outro: This brings our journey through Hattusa to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These stones have waited for centuries; let them keep waiting for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
